items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How do we ensure individual rights in our AI systems?
items.locator: Section 'What is the role of human oversight?', subsections 'How can we address risks of automation bias?' and 'How can we address risks of interpretability?'
items.quote: Those in charge of designing the front-end interface of an AI system must understand the needs, thought processes, and behaviours of human reviewers
items.why: Source of the quotation. Says controls against automation bias belong in the scoping and design phases, that interface options should be tested with reviewers early, that interpretability should be defined and measured for each system, and that a confidence score beside each output can help. Carries the banner that the guidance is under review because of the Data (Use and Access) Act; page metadata date 31 March 2026.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 25: Data protection by design and by default
items.quote: both at the time of the determination of the means for processing and at the time of the processing itself
items.why: The binding UK design duty: safeguards must be built into the processing when the means are chosen and while it runs. It covers personal data only and does not name human oversight; the regulator's guidance supplies that link.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.quote: enable the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller in relation to such decisions
items.why: A system that makes significant decisions solely by automated means must be set up so that a person can obtain human intervention. Inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; in force 5 February 2026. Applies only to significant, solely automated decisions using personal data.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 14: Human oversight
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use
items.why: The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page, HTTP 202). The duty is on the design of high-risk systems: interface tools, awareness of automation bias, the ability to disregard, override or reverse an output and to interrupt the system. The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus and the text shown is not yet updated; no paragraph is marked as amended.

items.title: Timeline for the Implementation of the EU AI Act
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: 02 Dec 2027 Rules for high-risk AI systems in Annex III apply
items.why: Basis for the statement that the design duty does not yet apply to the listed high-risk uses. A Commission summary; Article 113 point (c)(i) on the Service Desk gives the same date.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, Artificial intelligence toolkit: Human review
items.locator: First control measure, list of ways to meet expectations (fall back and hybrid working)
items.quote: Be flexible, so that in case of service failure, there is the option to move to a hybrid or manual model
items.why: The regulator's auditors expect a fall-back to manual or hybrid working, standard review procedures and testing of the review process on a sample of decisions. Carries the 'under review' banner; page metadata date 20 November 2024.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Principle 4: You have meaningful human control at the right stages
items.quote: This includes ensuring that humans validate any high-risk decisions influenced by AI and that you have strategies for meaningful intervention.
items.why: The government's standard for its own systems: where real-time review is not possible, human control must be placed at other stages, with routes for users to report issues and prompt a human review. Public sector only; cited as a UK benchmark.

items.title: Ethics, Transparency and Accountability Framework for Automated Decision-Making
items.locator: Section on explainability and human intervention
items.quote: Process owners need to introduce simple ways for the impacted person(s) to request human intervention or challenge a decision.
items.why: A seven-point framework for government use of automated decisions that treats the route to human intervention as something the process owner builds in. Public sector only. The date shown on the page is its last update, 29 November 2023.

items.title: Automation Bias in the AI Act: On the Legal Implications of Attempting to De-Bias Human Oversight of AI
items.publisher: Johann Laux and Hannah Ruschemeier (authors' copy on arXiv)
items.quote: the AIA's focus on providers does not adequately address design and context as causes of AB
items.why: Legal analysis of the AI Act's mention of automation bias: making overseers aware of the bias is not the same as designing it out, and the deployer's working context matters. Abstract read on arXiv; publication status in a journal was not checked.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: Processes for human oversight are defined, assessed, and documented in accordance with organizational policies from the GOVERN function.
items.why: International comparator. A voluntary US framework that treats human oversight as a designed and documented process, set when the system's context is mapped.
